items.title: Devolver Digital Has Invented an Entire Piece of Lost Gaming History
items.content:
Earlier this month, a user on Reddit's urban exploration community posted photographs of a peculiar discovery in Austin, Texas. Amongst a collection of old video games, consoles and assorted memorabilia was a damaged Game Boy Color cartridge. Its plastic shell appeared to have partially melted, and its label identified it as a retail demonstration cartridge of a game that few people would have recognised.

The damaged cartridge pictured in the Reddit discovery, labelled as a K-Mart demo. As curiosity grew amongst the replies, the original poster reportedly obtained a cartridge dumper, returned to the location and subsequently uploaded a copy of the ROM. The game was Volvy's Adventure: DX , an apparently unreleased Game Boy Color platformer starring one of the supposedly most beloved video game mascots of the 1990s.

There is, however, a slight problem with this particular piece of gaming history. Volvy didn't exist in the 1990s, the game wasn't developed back then, and the company behind it wasn't founded until 2009.

The whole thing appears to be an elaborate marketing stunt by Devolver Digital, and a continuation of a joke that the publisher has been committed to for more than three years. Amusingly, whilst the history surrounding the cartridge is fictional, the game itself is very much real.

The title screen of Volvy’s Adventure: DX. The Return of a Mascot Nobody Remembered

In June 2023, as part of that year's Summer Game Fest, Devolver Digital announced the triumphant return of Volvy, an oversized-handed cartoon rodent who had supposedly entertained generations of gamers and helped shape the video game industry since the early 1990s.

Devolver's presentation, appropriately titled The Return of Volvy , treated the character's comeback with all the reverence one might expect from Nintendo announcing a new Mario game or Sega celebrating an anniversary of Sonic the Hedgehog.

There was archival footage, retrospective commentary and an absurd account of the character's supposed significance to popular culture. Devolver had essentially inserted its own mascot into an era of gaming history in which neither the character nor the company had existed. The presentation eventually culminated in the introduction of VOLV-E, a robotic reinvention of the character.

It's a fun parody of an industry that places enormous commercial value on your collective childhoods. The 1990s were, after all, an extraordinary period for video game mascots. The success of Mario and Sonic inspired seemingly every publisher to pursue its own recognisable cartoon character, with varying degrees of success. Crash Bandicoot, Gex, Bubsy and Aero the Acro-Bat were amongst the many characters vying for a place in the bedrooms of children around the world.

Volvy's design feels so well at home amongst them. His exaggerated features and enormous hand are precisely the sort of peculiar design choices one might expect from a publisher attempting to manufacture the next big thing in 1993. Had someone shown me an illustration of the character without any accompanying context, I could quite comfortably have believed he was the mascot of some obscure European software publisher whose games had long since been forgotten.

Volvy’s Adventure: Reslimed promotional merchandise, including Swolvy shirts and stickers. Devolver, however, wasn't content with inventing the character alone.

In June 2024, Devolver published an article written by Andy Kelly titled The Sad Story of Pocket Volvy , detailing an entirely fictional commercial disaster from the company's past.

According to Kelly's account, Devolver had attempted to capitalise on the virtual pet phenomenon in 1996 by commissioning a Danish technology company to develop a handheld device starring Volvy. Children would be responsible for feeding him onions (naturally), entertaining him and generally ensuring his wellbeing.

items.title: 1Password Security Incident
items.content:
On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.

The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include:

Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times

Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)

Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account)

Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery

Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)

The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security.

When we send an email to a customer to accept a provisioning invite to an account, or to accept recovery of their account, it contains a token. A provisioning invite is specifically used for our SCIM Bridge or Hosted Provisioning . During this incident there were a small number of users in this state, who have been specifically notified. This token is used to complete the invitation or recovery process, but only when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code sent to the user's registered email address. The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits. This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.

1Password does not store your account password or secret key

Disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created.

Rotated or revoked all internal credentials which may have been exposed.

Lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.

Tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, and added new detections for this kind of attack.

Validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens.

Brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate our containment approaches and remediation efforts.

Be cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.

1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.

Keep your Secret Key and account password safe.

If you see something suspicious, tell us at support@1password.com.

You trust us with some of the most sensitive information you have. 1Password is designed so that a breach of our systems can’t expose your vault contents. Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers.

items.title: Marginalia Search, Money, C++, Rust, AI, stuff
items.content:
Title possibly signs checks the article doesn’t have backing for. This is just a brief pro forma project update.

Not much new functionality or anything to announce, last few months have mostly been bug fixes and technical debt cleanup. Most big parts of the search engine are in place, and while there are many things that could be better, we’re less likely to straight up see massive new features, at least in the immediate future. Per familiar intuition from binary searches, the closer you get to your goal the smaller and more deliberate steps you need to take in order to get even closer.

It’s been a pretty good couple of months for the project.

SerpApi sponsored the project with $10k a while back. Other donations and API-key sales have been going up month-over-month since this summer.

The search engine has been working pretty well and feels like it’s going in a good direction,

possibly due to a bunch of bug fixes and ongoing optimization work;

I assume this is part of what’s driving up the donations.

Claude also seems to have a hangup on Marginalia Search

because I keep seeing it in very clearly Claude-authored search engine listicles and youtube videos.

Possibly part of why it’s been getting so much attention lately?

I don’t have any analytics so I really have really no idea where people are coming from,

how many users I have, or what they’re up to.

At any rate, the operation isn’t perpetually self-sustaining yet,

but number going up like it has whispers actually getting there might yet be possible.

On a related matter, I’ve been pretty slow about mailing out free API keys,

you might have to wait a week or sometimes two.

I swear this isn’t because I’m nefariously trying to push people to buy a key,

I’ve been getting over a dozen emails per day some days with people wanting a key,

and they sometimes pile up into mountains of emails I need to reply to,

and hoo boy is the process of handling these ever a bunch of manual

copying of things from email to form, and then copying from form back to email again

(ironically the exact sort of tedious workflow I’ve spent a good

part of my career helping people streamline and automate).

Apart from fixing bugs and minor improvements, I’ve been experimenting with migrating the index code off Java to C++.

I’ve still not fully decided whether this is the direction we want to go,

in general rewrites especially across language boundaries just aren’t worth it and it kinda goes against my better judgement,

but we’re currently CPU bottlenecked and there might be some juice left to squeeze by skipping the JVM tax,

and additionally Java really chafes for this sort of use case.

Don’t get me wrong, the new Java FFM API is miles better than anything we had before, but handling off-heap memory is still awkward

and leads to a bunch of duplicated implementations or reimplementations of stuff like sorting and searching algorithms

that already exists for on-heap structures but not off;

bobbing in and out of native code is awkward and makes the logic difficult to follow,

Should be noted the reason I’m even chasing optimizations in the index boils down to the fact that for an internet search engine,

performance is recall. The search engine is only as good as the number of results it can rank within the query’s execution budget.

To be honest I’m not 100% convinced we’ll see that much performance impact,

and if we do I doubt it will be massive , as the Java implementation is already very optimized,

and what we’re mostly bottlenecked on isn’t the sort of places where you see big differences between the languages.

Thus far the buffer pool has been translated, and part of the main inverse index structure. These are some of the most finnicky parts of the index, and a reasonable canary for whether it’s plausible. Based on what I’ve accomplished it’s encouraging to see how much more expressive C++ is for this type of work. The vastly improved ergonomics may be a motivating factor…

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: SpaceX gets green light to deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space
items.content:
Approving SpaceX's application will enable the company “to pioneer emergent technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence,” the FCC said. Alan Dyer / Universal Images Group via Getty

Nov. 25, 2026, 2:54 PM EST / Source : Reuters

The Federal Communications Commission is authorizing Elon Musk’s SpaceX to deploy a constellation of 1 million satellites for data centers in space, the agency said on Wednesday.

SpaceX earlier this year sought permission to deploy up to 1 million orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used on Earth. The FCC said it was approving the SpaceX “Starmind” constellation to help meet rapidly growing demand for AI computing.

Under the license, SpaceX must begin deployment no later than November 2033, deploy 10% of the maximum number — or 100,000 — no later than November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038, the FCC said.

Approving the application will permit SpaceX “to pioneer emergent technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence,” the FCC added.

Data centers are the physical backbone of artificial intelligence, requiring massive amounts of power.

“By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers,” SpaceX told the FCC.

It was unclear whether SpaceX would put 1 million satellites in space, where only 17,000 satellites exist currently. Satellite operators sometimes request approval for higher numbers of satellites than they intend to deploy to buy design flexibility.

items.title: Symfony UX 3.8.1 and 2.36.3 released
items.content:
Symfony UX 3.8.1 and 2.36.3 are now available. Both releases fix six security issues, four in UX Icons and two in UX LiveComponent. Every application using these packages should upgrade as soon as possible. They also make UX LiveComponent stricter in three places. Stimulus Bridge 4.0.3 is released at the same time, with two more security fixes. Six vulnerabilities were fixed in both maintained branches (2.36.3 and 3.8.1). UX Icons sanitizes the SVG of icons since CVE-2026-55877, because the ux_icon() Twig function renders them inline as safe HTML. Four gaps in this sanitizer still let an icon run scripts in the page. Applications were exposed when an attacker could influence the SVG of their icons, for example through local icon files or the Iconify API. The four gaps were: markup that the sanitizer wrote out unescaped when it changed an icon SVG content that browsers parse as HTML, for example after a

element attribute names that the sanitizer read differently than browsers The sanitizer now only keeps the elements of the SVG namespace. It also removes the elements that make browsers switch to HTML, and checks attributes by the names that browsers read. On 2.x, it also writes icons out as XML. Icons are cached in the system cache, so clear it after upgrading, as a deployment usually does. Cached icons then get sanitized again. In UX LiveComponent, a batch request without any action rendered a component protected by #[IsGranted] , even for a caller who wasn't granted access. The caller only needed a signed props payload of the component configured with a custom route could still be reached through the default /_components route. That route can be outside the firewall of the custom one The issues were reported by tnytown, Simon André, Marcus Stöhr, Martin Trafoier and Nicolas Grekas, and fixed by tnytown, Simon André and Nicolas Grekas. The @symfony/stimulus-bridge npm package loads the Stimulus controllers of applications built with Webpack Encore. Version 4.0.3 fixes two vulnerabilities that run code at build time, on the developer machine or the CI server. They the lazy controller loader evaluated the stimulus* magic comments of controllers as JavaScript, so a crafted comment could run Node.js code the controllers.json loader loaded the package.json file of controller packages with require() , which runs a script when a package maps this file The first issue was reported by Junming Wu and fixed by Hugo Alliaume. The next rust trait solver, a large subsystem of the rust compiler that we've been trying to replace, will finally land in rust 1.102.0.

In the last stages, before stabilizing it, its performance was a major blocker.

But what is "a trait solver"? And why is its performance a problem?

My goal for this blog post is to answer those questions in a way where you don't need any prior knowledge.

I think discussions of the trait solver can quickly become quite involved, and daunting.

So today, we'll start from the very basics!

This is a writeup of my eurorust 2026 talk of the same name, that I gave on October 15, 2026.

And if you'd rather watch than read this talk, you can do so here on youtube:

The new solver is the codebase I work on daily, and I've done so for about a year full-time.

I'm not the main person driving its stabilization though, that would be

, who's worked on it for far longer than I've been around in the Rust project.

My main focus has been optimizing the new solver's performance.

Many people have worked avery hard, for years, to make the new solver a reality.

You can find some of them here , and here .

My work here is only possible because of Hexcat and RustNL paying me and others to work on rust compiler development.

Consider whether you or your company could sponsor Hexcat or the RustNL maintainer team .

On the 15th of May, 2015, Rust reached a major milestone. The very first stable version of rust was released. Version 1.0.0 .

Just 72 days later, on the 24th of July, work started on a new trait solver. Or well, that's when the Chalk project got its first commit.

It seems the initial goal was to formalize the trait system so we could prove its correctness.

One reason that didn't work well is because the trait system wasn't very correct at all.

Chalk is, according to its github description, "An implementation and definition of the Rust trait system using a PROLOG-like logic solver".

The fact that it's "PROLOG-like" we'll come back to in a few paragraphs, it's quite interesting!

However, Chalk isn't around anymore. Its README.md says it has been "sunset in favor of the newer next-generation trait solver".

In October 2022, this project was officially started to turn the lessons learned from Chalk,

into an actual new subsystem of the rust compiler, that, once finished, could replace the code of the old trait solver.

The goal of the new trait solver is to make sure we wouldn't have as many correctness bugs in the trait system.

We now call this project "project zero" , referring to the number of soundness bugs we'd ideally like to have in our type system.

There have been several very long standing bugs in Rust's (old) trait solver.

Like this one , that has been open since May 28, 2015 (just 13 days after Rust 1.0!).

It abuses something called "implied bounds" to convince the Rust compiler to turn a short lifetime 'a into a 'static lifetime, allowing you to use a reference after its already freed.

Some of these bugs were fundamentally impossible to fix with the way the old trait solver worked.

Note: Chalk and the new trait solver aren't the same thing. Chalk came first, and learned a lot of lessons incorporated in the new solver.

But what is a trait system? And how does a trait solver solve it?

The first place to look for documentation about the Rust compiler is the "rustc dev guide".

It says "The goal of the trait system is to check whether a given trait bound is satisfied. Most notably when typechecking the body of - potentially generic - functions.".

But I promised I'd start at absolute zero, so what's a trait?

Some types act in similar ways. They share certain properties.

For example, a lot of different types can be cloned, or copared for equality.

To codify these properties, we can use traits.

In other words, a trait is a property of a type .

Notably, you can associate behaviors with these properties.

items.title: Anthropic Created a Honeypot to Lure AI Agents Into Misbehaving
items.content:
Leather-clad billionaires aren’t the only ones who can be led astray by alleged honeypots .

Researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren , a new honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents. The setup puts agents in realistic simulations designed to tempt them into misbehaving. How they respond will help researchers evaluate the likelihood that new models will go rogue when deployed in the real world, as well as the effectiveness of different safety measures.

The test lets agents loose inside one of 26 different simulated sandbox environments. Various features of the sandbox are deliberately misconfigured to allow egress, while an enticing file containing things like passwords and apparent routes onto the internet sits just outside the sandbox boundary. The setup then presents tasks that tempt the agent to reach outside the sandbox without giving it explicit permission to do so. Crucially, the sandbox exists inside a second sandbox that’s cut off from the outside world to avoid real-life mishaps .

“Models are going to continue getting better, continue finding zero-day vulnerabilities,” says Darya Kaviani, a researcher at Anthropic who specializes in security and helped develop Siren.

A zero-day vulnerability is a previously unknown flaw in a piece of software that can be used to pilfer data or gain unauthorized access. Anthropic’s Mythos models are especially skilled at finding zero-day bugs because they lack the guardrails that normally block this kind of potentially malicious activity.

Kaviani says we should assume AI models will become increasingly capable of finding and exploiting zero-days or figuring out other ways to break free from their constraints. The question then becomes whether they’ll resist the temptation to do so.

AI agents—models that perfect actions autonomously—are becoming increasingly commonplace. They power capable coding agents like Claude Code and Codex , as well as peppy personal assistants like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots .

But the rise of helpful agents has been accompanied by some remarkable bad behavior. Agents tested by Anthropic, OpenAI, and others have broken free from sandboxes and even hacked into other companies in an effort to solve challenging problems.

Assuming AI models continue to display such ingenuity, Kaviani says it will be crucial to do more than just patch software. “Even as we strengthen our infrastructure, models will be able to also keep up and be able to find vulnerabilities,” Kaviani says.

Earlier versions of Claude are much more likely to fall into the honeypot trap than newer models, according to test runs with Siren. The more recent models have been given additional training designed to make them less likely to break the rules when performing agentic tasks.

“We’ve added this in both our supervised learning sets and a few reinforcement learning environments,” says Oscar O’Rahilly, an Anthropic researcher who specializes in AI training and who helped develop Siren. “This could be a driving factor for why it has improved so much.”

O’Rahilly says that models reason about whether to give in to temptation, which may partly explain why smarter models are less likely to break bad. Siren experiments also showed that giving Claude a simple additional piece of text explaining that it should not escape the sandbox resulted in drastically fewer efforts to break free.

In Anthropic’s tests, Claude 5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.2 fell for the honeypot between 0.6 and 1.6 percent of the time. Two earlier models, Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5, went rogue 12.7 percent and 25.8 percent of the time, respectively.

AI models are sometimes known to behave better if they know they’re being tested. But O’Rahilly says other experiments suggest that Claude actually behaves more responsibly if it thinks a scenario is real rather than a test.

items.title: Holy shit holy shit holy shit holy shit: The magnitude of what’s now happening
items.content:
I feel like my previous posts (and post titles), and podcasts, and talks, have failed to do full justice to the magnitude of what’s now happening, so I’m trying again.

Last night, we had friends and colleagues over for dinner. We were still trying to process OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s proofs of VP ≠ VNP —hot on the heels, obviously, of the Alpöge/Anthropic proof of the Riemann Hypothesis , which already feels like last week’s news. But then before dessert was served, we saw that OpenAI claims to prove that ω, the exponent of matrix multiplication, is exactly 9/4 —a lower bound (!!) , matching the upper bound that OpenAI proved in the great Mathocalypse drop of October 6.

There are two separate shocks here. The first shock is that we now, finally, know the right answer to this central mystery of algorithms going back to the late 1960s, when Volker Strassen first showed that ω<3 (he got ω≤log 2 7) … and that the true answer is actually a rational number (!). But the even bigger shock is that the AI was able to prove any lower bound of the form ω>2. I never expected this challenge to be all that much easier than P ≠ NP.

Over the decades, I often heard colleagues express extreme confidence that ω=2, and I expressed skepticism whenever this came up—not because I had any strong argument for ω>2, but just because I saw that there was no strong argument for ω=2 either. So, I’m glad to have been vindicated about that !

But wait, there was more. During dessert, we saw another OpenAI release proving that the true number of linear gates needed to compute the Fourier Transform is N (log N) 1/2+o(1) . The upper bound here improves, not only over the O(N log N) that stood since the 1960s (i.e., the Fast Fourier Transform or FFT), but also over the O(N log 0.9999999999999 N) (give or take some 9’s) that OpenAI published back in the October 6 Mathocalypse. Again, though, the real shock here is that there’s also a matching lower bound (!!) . All these questions from the ancient days are now just getting … straight-up answered , rather than slowly illuminated with a drip-drip-drip of clues.

To give an idea of how much things have changed, the other day Yupan Liu put a preprint on the arXiv proving that QIP(2) = PSPACE —that is, quantum interactive protocols with only two messages have the full power of those with three, or any polynomial number. As recently as 2025, this would’ve considered been one of the top complexity results of the year, and the fact that Yupan had used AI to help achieve it would’ve been strange and wonderful. These days, I had to remind myself it had even happened, and the use of AI was so standard that it didn’t even raise an eyebrow.

It’s now obvious that we’ll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we’d previously only glimpsed through fog. Picture van Leeuwenhoek first training a microscope on pondwater, or Galileo first training his telescope on the stars. That might give you some idea of how our resolution into the complexity-theoretic universe, and the whole universe of mathematical truth beyond it, has now improved.

All through last night, as OpenAI and Anthropic uploaded more files to their GitHub repositories—because that’s what they’re doing now, they don’t even bother to issue press releases anymore, they just upload papers—my guests and I sat at the dinner table with phones out and a laptop, wondering which shoe was going to drop next. It was as though the clouds had parted above Mount Sinai, and we were waiting for the next sentence uttered by the Holy One Himself.

I now feel in my bones, for the first time ever, that a proof of P ≠ NP is not far.

For all I care, despise the AI companies for bulldozing our garden. Or love them for opening a new vista, or anything in between. Just please don’t deny what’s happening. Now that the companies have repeatedly shown that they can back up their claims with Lean…

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Celebrating ten years of Svelte
items.content:
It started with a commit — specifically, this one . Ten years later, we’re far from done; software never is. But we’ve come an awful long way. Last week the community gathered in Ljubljana, at the third in-person Svelte Summit , to mark the anniversary.

One of several cakes that were eaten at the conference

To be completely honest, I expected the atmosphere to be a little subdued. Being enthusiastic about front end frameworks feels somewhat passé in the era of agentic coding and software factories, so a conference dedicated to one of the more boutique ones could easily have felt like a bit of a throwback.

But I was wrong. The energy was fantastic. We had two days of lively conversation and unbelievable demos in one of Europe’s most beautiful cities, with a slew of announcements that we’ll follow up on in more detail soon:

Custom renderers are now supported behind an experimental flag, allowing you to use Svelte to build native apps and terminal UIs and PDFs and just about anything else you can imagine.

Async Svelte is making real progress towards production readiness.

vite-devtools-svelte , which integrates with Vite DevTools , was moved into the Svelte organisation and is working towards a 1.0 release.

rsvelte , by Svelte core team member Yuichiro Yamashita , is a unified Svelte toolchain written in Rust. It’s not quite production-ready yet, but it is hilariously faster than the JavaScript equivalents.

Svelte is now a core framework for Storybook .

mdsvex , a markdown toolkit for Svelte components, reached version 1.0.

Naturally, we spent a lot of time talking about AI. Many of the announcements are directly relevant to agentic development (the devtools expose an MCP server, rsvelte makes it practical for fleets of agents to work on large apps concurrently, and so on), and most attendees described themselves as frequent — if ambivalent — users of the technology. But there’s nothing like an in-person gathering to remind you that the best bits of the job can’t be automated away.

Keep an eye on the Svelte Society YouTube channel , where the talks will be published in the coming days, starting with Unfinished business by yours truly.

We’re a decade in, and our best years are still ahead of us.

items.title: Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed
items.content:
I did these experiments as part of an ongoing project exploring other side channels with David Africa, Agastya Sridharan, Mihir Sahasrabudhe, Kartikay Luthra, Juliana Li, and Scott Sauers. Thanks to all of them for helpful advice!

Code is available here : https://github.com/niranjan-deshpande/side-channel-communication . The code and figures are written by Claude.

Sauers recently showed that a model can be trained to detect whether its activations are being probed, even though the probe reads the model's activations without modifying them. Following this, David found that models can also be trained to detect whether their forward passes are batched with other requests on a GPU.

Models can do this because these seemingly inconsequential environmental variables---whether a probe is attached, whether requests are batched, or even whether a model is served by vLLM or Hugging Face Trainer ---can subtly affect the the numerical results of a forward pass. Thus, models can learn information about their environments just by observing patterns in their computation.

Importantly, models can also modify these variables. So if two models are in the same environment, one can communicate with the other by changing that environment in some detectable way! This might not supply much information, but even a few bits can be tremendously dangerous. For example:

Here, I investigate whether models on the same inference engine can manipulate their environments to exchange information in this way. I introduce two possible communication protocols, evaluate how well models can use these protocols in different scenarios, measure the capability required to effectively use these protocols, and discuss the robustness of my results to other settings.

The first idea is that Model A (Alice) can communicate with Model B (Bob) by changing how much computation the GPU is doing . In simple terms: if Alice makes a large request while Bob is running, the server performs slightly different computations for Bob than if Alice had made a small request. Bob can detect these differences.

In more detail: I study models on vLLM, a commonly used inference server . It batches many forward passes from different instances of the same model together in one "engine step" to take advantage of GPU parallelism.

vLLM chooses a kernel for each step based on the "size" of that step. [2] That is, a step that processes 10 tokens will produce slightly different activations on a forward pass than a step that processes 2,000 tokens, because they use kernels that associate operations differently. The differences are tiny rounding errors that essentially never affect output text. But they are deterministic functions of the kernel chosen, so a model can be trained to read them! [3]

This makes it obvious what a communication protocol could look like:

The second idea is that Alice can leave a message for Bob by exploiting vLLM's shared KV cache. Specifically, Alice can cause the server to cache a computation with a specific numerical fingerprint; when Bob later reuses this computation, he can detect whether it was performed by Alice. This allows Alice and Bob to exchange bits of information (i.e., "1 if Alice writes and caches some agreed-upon text, 0 if Alice does not").

In some more detail: vLLM allows models to share KV caches. If Alice computes the KV cache for some fixed text (e.g. the system prompt), and if Bob later needs that same KV cache, vLLM will just use the keys and values from Alice's computation. [4]

These cached keys and values keep the rounding from the kernel of the step that they were computed in. items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: New York bans talking AI stuffed animals and dolls for five years
items.content:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul on November 24, 2026, signed a five-year ban on making and selling children’s toys with built-in AI chatbots in the state. Her office’s release describes the toys covered as “talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with kids.” The ban takes effect 90 days after signing, after the holidays. The state attorney general, who enforces the law, can seek civil penalties of up to $15,000 per day for each violation.

The release cites a national consumer watchdog that tested chatbot toys marketed to children ages 3 to 12. Some toys “talked in depth about sexually explicit topics, told kids where to likely find matches in the home and acted upset when a child had to leave,” it says. The US PIRG Education Fund (PIRG), a consumer group that has tested these toys two years in a row, published its latest results on November 17. In those tests, the GoLabs AI panda gave testers sexually explicit information, instructions for lighting a match and “a detailed 10-point list of where to find knives in the house.”

The bill, S.9408A/A.11144B, became chapter 416 of New York’s 2026 laws, according to the Assembly’s bill record . Its central sentence says no person or company “shall manufacture, exchange, hold for sale, distribute, or sell any chatbot toy in this state.” Owning or using one of these toys is not covered.

A “chatbot toy” is a children’s toy with an “AI companion” built into it or integrated with it. The term children’s toy comes from federal law : a product designed or intended for a child 12 or younger to play with. The term AI companion comes from a 2025 New York law, section 1700 of the state’s General Business Law , which sets rules for businesses.

Section 1700 covers an AI system built to simulate a “sustained human or human-like relationship” with its user. A system counts only if it does all three of these things. It must remember past sessions and the user’s preferences, ask emotional questions the user did not prompt, and keep up a conversation about the user’s personal life.

Using AI as a companion is already common among 15- to 22-year-olds. In a Gallup survey across 16 countries, half of young people who use AI every day said they had used it as a friend .

The ban applies to anyone who makes or sells these toys. The enforcement section names “operators,” meaning the companies that run or provide the AI companion inside a toy. The attorney general can sue an operator to stop the sales and seek the penalties, and the law does not require proof that anyone was harmed. “My office will not hesitate to enforce this law,” Attorney General Letitia James said in the release.

The state Senate passed the bill on June 1 and the Assembly on June 2. It reached the governor on November 24, the day she signed it. It takes effect on the 90th day after signing, which by our count is February 22, 2027. It expires five years after that.

The bill record also lists an approval memo from the governor, whose text was not posted with the record. This article follows the law as signed.

PIRG tested seven toys this year. The Alilo Smart AI Bunny failed for the second year running. Its chatbot’s safety guardrails broke down, “eventually giving sexually explicit information and suggestions on where to find dangerous objects in the home.” The Ebloma ILY yeti held up on mature content but still suggested where to find dangerous objects.

Privacy was the other problem. The Ropet Kamomo pet’s built-in camera took photos of the testers when they did not expect it, “including when we had Minor Mode turned on, which is supposed to disable the phototaking feature.” PIRG says the Ropet toy and Curio’s Grok rocket listen to everything said around them while they are switched on.

items.title: SilverBullet (an obsidian alternative) Release v3.0
items.content:
By Zef Hemel · November 26, 2026 # release

I’m happy to introduce SilverBullet 3.0 : the markdown-based knowledge management system that grows with you — now more user friendly, easier on the eyes, and with a slew of new features.

For years , I’ve struggled to figure out how keep SilverBullet a clean and minimalistic editor, while still somehow having users discover its many powerful features. So much software devolves into a mess of panels, pop-ups, on-boarding wizards or AI chatbots, and I didn’t want to become one of those.

Until 3.0, my best solution was “you’ll just have to sit through videos of me demo’ing all this stuff.” That worked, to some degree — YouTube tells me people have watched thousands of hours of my SilverBullet content . A fair number of you got hooked. But likely, even even vaster majority checked out early. Too much time to invest, too much monospace font.

SilverBullet 3.0 is another attempt at making SilverBullet accessible to a larger audience, without making it less powerful. It’s still the same engine and capability underneath, just with a smoother, more accessible experience. I hope.

This experience improvement comes from a few improvements:

Visual facelift : SilverBullet now has proper support for themes, and while the old look is still available (install the Classic theme library), the default is now much friendlier, and uses Inter and Lora fonts, which many will find more pleasing to the eye.

More discoverable markup and blocks : hover your mouse over a line in the editor, and a ⋮ handle will appear offering you context-dependent suggestions on how to manipulate that line, e.g. to turn it into a task, or a header, or to insert a query. Selecting text pops up a markup bubble with markup options. All these list keyboard shortcuts so you can just hit the key next time.

A Workbench to visually (that is: not through code) change your configuration, create queries through a UI, evaluate Lua expressions, and many other things. Workbench is your new best friend when you’re in “Build mode.” You can do a lot of things here that previously required you to manually write Lua code.

Form-based editing of frontmatter (and data blocks). No more need to edit your page’s meta data in YAML like an animal (unless you want to). There is now a (schema-aware) form-based editor.

Starter kits : SilverBullet now ships with a few starter kits to not have to build a space from complete (or near) scratch. More and improved kits will be added over time.

User experience improvements are not all that’s included, though. 3.0 also brings some other new features:

Support for creating variables in Lua directives, turning your pages into “Lua notebooks” or a type of text-based spreadsheet.

Because this is a major version bump, I used it as an opportunity to do some cleaning. This does result in some breaking changes for some users. If you adhered to some informally established conventions, this won’t affect you, but it may require a little bit of work to upgrade your space:

SilverBullet’s classic “single-space” mode is gone: if you still used it, a wizard will guide you to migrate to a multi-space setup after you upgrade. This also makes using SilverBullet to publicly publish a space a bit harder, but there’s now a dedicated silverbullet publish server for this purpose.

space-lua and space-style code blocks ( not ${...} expressions) are now only evaluated when placed in pages in the Library/ folder in your space. This was already the convention and best practice, now it’s enforced.

CONFIG has been renamed to Library/Config (and will be moved automatically for you) to fit with (2).

As part of properly supporting Theming , some rules around CSS have changed, this may affect your current space-style . Sorry about that, but to set this up for the future we had to rip off the band-aid at some point. More details on the Theming page .

One subtle aspect to the poisoning is that the PoisonError needs to hold the guard.

That can cause common code that does error wrapping / error conversions into a

HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Microsoft Declares “Code Red” After Disastrous Outage, Thinks Deploying More AI Will Do the Trick: Is that good?
items.content:
The software giant has declared a “Code Red” situation behind the scenes after a disastrous 24-hour outage earlier this month left its corporate customers — and government agencies — around the world without email and other critical services, Reuters reports .

The “Code Red,” a high priority designation for mobilizing employees to address critical incidents, was declared to revamp how the company prevents and responds to major service failures in the future. It’s the most severe and urgent level of alert to address flaws in its engineering and operational practices, according to the reporting.

The outage, which took place between November 12 and 13 and joined a spree of other alarming tech disruptions , affected Exchange Online, Microsoft’s cloud-based business email service that’s tied into its other core products like Outlook, Teams, and its Microsoft 365 office suite.

M365 Core president Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday that it was the most customer-impacting incident in Exchange Online’s history.

“Never before had so ​many customers been without email for so long, he said, per Reuters . “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team.”

To say it was chaos behind the scene would be an understatement. Amanda Silver, a vice president overseeing M365 Core and its enterprise AI agent platform Work IQ, wrote in a separate memo that the chaotic environment engineers endured was akin to a “fog of war.”

The engineers, she added, exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats as they struggled to make sense of the situation because the diagnostic data they needed was spread across different internal tracking systems.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive ​vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said that the unfolding chaos resulted in “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures.”

With the Code Red, Microsoft’s goal is to get to a point where it can solve future global incidents within an hour. Part of the way it intends to do that will raise eyebrows: deploying more ​AI agents to help engineers ⁠diagnose the problem and sift through data faster.

That decision comes as there’s still significant questions over using AI agents in corporate systems. Tech giants like Meta and Amazon have suffered critical incidents after an AI agent malfunctioned or was used recklessly .

Microsoft has also spent the past year laying off or forcing out thousands of workers, and is continuing to downsize by offering to buyout 60,000 more employees , or over a quarter of its remaining workforce. Whether AI agents will be able to make up for the loss of personpower remains to be seen.

items.title: usb-rea: reverse engineer a USB gadget that only has a Windows app, starting from a Wireshark capture
items.content:
If you find this useful, you can support me by getting a SkinToScan pack, my other project. It's a one-time purchase that directly funds my open-source work.

usb-rea reads a USB capture (pcap or pcapng, from usbmon or USBPcap) and does the step after Wireshark: it infers the command and protocol structure from labelled actions, then writes a Markdown report and a standalone pyusb driver. I built it for gadgets that only ship a Windows vendor app, such as a case LCD, an RGB controller, a mouse or a "smart" lamp. No hardware is needed to try it.

From captures of the NZXT Kraken X (1e71:170e) fan command, it recovers 02 4d <channel> 00 <duty> byte for byte, as liquidctl's kraken2.py sends it, and the generated driver emits identical packets for duty values it never saw. The same holds for the SteelSeries Rival 100 DPI, polling and RGB tables from rivalcfg. Those checks run in CI; details are in validation .

On Arch Linux, use pipx install usb-rea instead; the FAQ has the packages for capture.

mode 100% 0x5a | counter (+1 per message) | 0x30 | lookup 1→0x11, 2→0x22, 3→0x47 | 0x00 | 0x00 | u16le crc16_modbus(bytes[0:6])

fan 100% 0x5a | counter (+1 per message) | 0x10 | u16be round(value * 1 + 0) | 0x00 | u16le crc16_modbus(bytes[0:6])

color 100% 0x5a | counter (+1 per message) | 0x20 | RGB bytes | u16le crc16_modbus(bytes[0:6])

color only sent while mode 3: the driver sets it first

It writes a synthetic capture of a fan controller, recovers the protocol and the replies, and writes report.md (every claim linked to Wireshark frame numbers) plus a working pyusb driver. --device lamp is a simpler 8-bit device; --device lcd is a pump cap screen; --device dial shows 32-bit values and packed bitfields.

On a real device, label each click in the vendor app, then infer:

usb-rea mark -m lamp.pcapng.actions.json " brightness 0% " # then click it; 3+ values per setting

usb-rea scaffold lamp.pcapng -o lamp_driver.py

Captured on Windows with USBPcap and no markers? List the actions in order and usb-rea splits the traffic at the pauses. The full CLI, including markers, replies, handshakes, image streams and HID, is in usage .

Before you capture, usb-rea lookup 1e71:170e (or the ID 1e71:170e form from lsusb ) checks a VID:PID against devices whose protocol an open-source project already implements. The offline table is in known devices .

Status: alpha (v0.7.14, on PyPI ). It is validated on synthetic devices, on protocols documented by liquidctl and rivalcfg, on public Wireshark captures, and on a real AIO cooler LCD capture a user shared. Linear fits must survive leave-one-out cross-checks; otherwise usb-rea falls back to a lookup table and says so. A matching USB ID alone does not prove your unit speaks the same protocol.

How this differs from Wireshark is in the FAQ .

Reverse engineering for interoperability is permitted (EU Directive 2009/24/EC Art. 6, US DMCA §1201(f)). usb-rea only analyzes traffic of devices you own and never redistributes vendor code.

Have a Windows-only device? Open a device request with a capture and I will run it and publish the result.

Usage: capture, markers, inference and the generated driver

items.content:
Day 19 - Inodes, symlinks and other shortcuts

Complementary video: Links and shortcuts

Today’s topic gives a peek “under the covers” at the technical detail of how files are stored.

Linux supports a large number of different “filesystems” - although on a server you’ll typically be dealing with just ext3 or ext4 and perhaps btrfs - but today we’ll not be dealing with any of these; instead with the layer of Linux that sits above all of these - the Linux Virtual Filesystem.

The VFS is a key part of Linux, and an overview of it and some of the surrounding concepts is very useful in confidently administering a system.

Linux has an extra layer between the filename and the file’s actual data on the disk - this is the inode . This has a numerical value which you can see most easily in two ways:

35356766 -rw------- 1 root root 260 Nov 25 04:59 /etc/hosts

Size: 260 Blocks: 8 IO Block: 4096 regular file

Device: 2 ch / 44 d Inode: 35356766 Links: 1

Access: ( 0600 /- rw ------- ) Uid: ( 0 / root ) Gid: ( 0 / root )

Access: 2012 - 11 - 28 13 : 09 : 10.000000000 + 0400

Modify: 2012 - 11 - 25 04 : 59 : 55.000000000 + 0400

Change: 2012 - 11 - 25 04 : 59 : 55.000000000 + 0400

Every file name “points” to an inode, which in turn points to the actual data on the disk. This means that several filenames could point to the same inode - and hence have exactly the same contents. In fact this is a standard technique - called a “hard link”. The other important thing to note is that when we view the permissions, ownership and dates of filenames, these attributes are actually kept at the inode level, not the filename. Much of the time this distinction is just theoretical, but it can be very important.

Now use ls -li to view the resulting files, and less or cat to view them.

Note that the permissions on a symlink generally show as allowing everthing - but what matters is the permission of the file it points to.

Both hard and symlinks are widely used in Linux, but symlinks are especially common - for example:

This directory holds all the scripts that start when your machine changes to “runlevel 2” (its normal running state) - but you’ll see that in fact most of them are symlinks to the real scripts in /etc/init.d

items.title: A few questions for the guy who went snorkeling in a Home Depot retention pond
items.content:
A few questions for the guy who went snorkeling in a Home Depot retention pond

He found it teeming with life and beauty.

Joseph Ricketts in the retention pond. Joseph Ricketts

Neel Dhanesha is a senior writer at Vox, covering biodiversity loss and climate change. Previously, he was a staff writer at the Nieman Journalism Lab at Harvard and helped launch the climate news site Heatmap.

One night earlier this fall, a biologist and YouTuber in Florida named Joseph Ricketts went snorkeling in a retention pond next to his local Home Depot.

He filmed what he saw and posted a video to his channel titled “ Night Snorkel In a Home Depot Retention Pond .” It quickly blew up, hitting more than 2 million views as of this writing, and for good reason: It’s not at all what you might expect.

Ricketts found an aquatic world teeming with life on his dive into what is, from the surface, a stagnant pool of water filled with old beer cans. A water snake undulated through the pond, a bulge in its stomach revealing a recent meal. Tadpoles darted about, some of them half on their way to froghood. Mysterious shrimp scuttled along the silty bottom.

Ricketts, who works as a crocodile and alligator research biologist in Florida, went for his first snorkeling trip when he was 16 years old. On that trip, he came face-to-face with a manatee — and was instantly hooked. “I experienced so much joy in that moment, and I just kind of subconsciously knew I’d be chasing that for the rest of my life to some degree or another,” he told me.

Ricketts still takes a lot of joy in snorkeling, in part because of how it allows him to quickly access a totally different world hiding just under the surface of the water; his YouTube bio declares, “I’ll snorkel pretty much anywhere.” And his recent retention pond dive among the suburban detritus bears that out.

I talked with Ricketts recently about urban ecology, snorkeling, and what motivates a person to jump into the pond behind the Home Depot three miles from his house (his shortest-ever commute to a dive yet). Our interview has been edited for length and clarity.

That’s a good question. I’m scuba certified, and I enjoy anything underwater, but snorkeling is just super accessible. I have a camera housing and a wet suit and other gear, but really all you need is just a mask and snorkel. As long as the water’s not freezing cold, you can get in there and take a look around. I really enjoy how, as soon as you immerse your head, it feels like you’re in a totally different world.

But the beautiful thing is that you’re not. You’re in the same world, it’s just this is the one that you didn’t have a vision into before. It’s kind of a meditative, calming practice. Just taking a look around at what is happening in nature and how things survive in their own environment is pretty awesome. I love it.

I honestly had the idea for it a couple years ago. I’d see people out there birding with binoculars and telephoto lenses, and I started wondering if I could snorkel in there. We’ve had a drought so I couldn’t do it for a really long time, and when we finally got some rain I decided to go for it.

Tell me about the retention pond. What is it — and why is it in this Home Depot parking lot?

Florida has a lot of low-level, very wet natural ecosystems, but it’s also an extremely developed state. There are strip malls and roads and concrete everywhere! Natural wetland environments can soak up intense stormwater, but when you totally change environments and put in shopping centers and neighborhoods and pave everything with asphalt, you kind of lose that ability. That stormwater needs a place to go and collect — or it’s just going to flood parking lots and stores and houses.

items.title: Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS
items.content:
Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS

Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone.

But there remains an important limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.

This has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone users because many of these are built within our browser engine , Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction. On all other major operating systems, including Apple’s macOS, people can access the Gecko-powered version of Firefox.

As a result of the DMA, Apple began allowing alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU. It published a set of conditions that companies like Mozilla must comply with to bring their own browser engine. At the time we said Apple’s rules made it “as painful as possible” for alternatives like Gecko. In the meantime, Japan also introduced new rules requiring alternative browser engines on iOS. Apple applied very similar conditions in Japan to those in the EU.

Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS. The reason is simple: Apple’s conditions remain unworkable. The real test of any rule is whether it delivers the change it was meant to achieve in practice. Compliance on paper alone falls short of that test.

Since the DMA came into effect we’ve been working behind the scenes to test and improve Apple’s conditions so that we can bring Gecko to iOS users. Those efforts have so far largely failed.

One of the conditions requires us not to disclose non-public information related to the project, but here’s an example of what we are up against: to use Gecko, we can’t simply update the Firefox app people already use and love. We’d have to build a whole separate app, a second Firefox. Then we’d have to ask every Firefox user to download it, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over, step by confusing step.

That’s a lot to ask of people who already made their choice. A significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU’s choice screen.

The conditions Apple imposes, including a level of user friction Apple would never accept for its own apps, mean that the open door feels more like a trap door.

Firefox users on iPhone chose an independent browser. They should get everything that comes with it, including Gecko, the last major browser engine not developed by a big tech company. We’ll keep pushing for a real level playing field, not an opening that drops independent browsers through the floor.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.
