items.title: OpenProject wins contract as Jira replacement in German federal administration
items.content:
From Jira to OpenProject: A major milestone for digital sovereignty in Germany

Published by Birthe Lindenthal November 24, 2026 Estimated reading time: 5 minutes

Some days remind us why we do what we do.

We are incredibly happy to share that OpenProject has been awarded the contract for the provision of an open source issue tracking solution in a Europe-wide tender issued by the Informationstechnikzentrum Bund (ITZBund), the German Federal Government’s central IT service provider.

The framework agreement covers the provision of OpenProject as an open source alternative to Atlassian Jira, including migration services, training, support, and further development.

For us, this is much more than winning a tender. It is a confirmation of the path we have chosen, a recognition of the hard work our team and Community have put into OpenProject, and an encouraging signal for the entire European open source ecosystem.

And yes, this is definitely a moment worth celebrating!

Over the past months, we have been working intensively on making OpenProject an increasingly powerful alternative to Atlassian Jira. We have spoken to numerous organizations, listened to their requirements, and gained a deep understanding of the challenges involved in moving away from established proprietary solutions.

With Atlassian’s announcement to discontinue Jira Data Center in March 2029, the question of how to move forward has become increasingly urgent for many organizations.

But replacing Jira is not simply about finding another issue tracker. Large organizations have built complex environments over many years, with numerous projects, customized workflows, integrations, automations, and established ways of working.

A successful transition requires a reliable migration path, enterprise-ready functionality, and a long-term perspective.

This is precisely what we have been working on. Our recent and upcoming developments reflect the progress we have made:

A dedicated Jira migration tool to facilitate the transition from existing Jira Data Center environments to OpenProject.

Enhanced agile project management capabilities, including redesigned backlogs, sprint management, and multiple active sprints.

Project-specific work package IDs, custom fields, and configurable workflows.

Upcoming type variants and reusable workflows and forms , enabling project-specific configurations while maintaining consistency across teams and projects.

A dedicated approach to migrating ScriptRunner for Jira Data Center .

A growing ecosystem of open source integrations, enabling seamless collaboration across applications.

AI integration through our Model Context Protocol (MCP) server , giving organizations the freedom to choose their AI models.

There is still plenty of work ahead of us, and we are tackling it at full speed. But receiving this level of trust from Germany’s central federal IT service provider is a confirmation that we are moving in the right direction.

Digital sovereignty is becoming a reality

Digital sovereignty has been discussed for years. What is particularly exciting right now is seeing these discussions translate into concrete decisions. Germany’s federal administration is taking an important step towards greater technological independence by investing in open source solutions. For public institutions, the ability to decide where software runs, how data is managed, who maintains the software, and how it evolves is fundamental. It is about retaining the freedom to make independent technological decisions today and in the future.

With OpenProject, organizations can operate their project management software on their own infrastructure, inspect the source code, integrate it into their existing IT landscape, and actively participate in its further development. Digital sovereignty means having access to mature, reliable, and interoperable solutions without becoming dependent on a single vendor.

items.title: Why your software development isn't speeding up
items.content:
Organizations are starting to notice that individual gains from LLM-based AI tools disappear swiftly. They just don’t make it downstream to where they matter. What this should make engineering leaders realize is that their way of thinking about software delivery is wrong.

There’s a near-universal belief that developers are the constraining factor in software change throughput. This is wrong. Writing code is not the constraint, and it never was . Whenever I’ve worked on a team to reduce the amount of work they tackle at once, I’ve seen their team-level productivity climb immediately into zones many organizations can only dream of.

Alone, the team-level boost is meaningless unless the changes they make can smoothly flow all the way to the people who need them.

Flipping team-level productivity into an organization-level improvement means carrying the change through to the end. That change must be validated to whatever standard the organization requires, it needs to be deployed to production, and it must be switched on for users to try, so you can see how well it solves their problems.

The organizations outperforming their peers with AI are the same organizations that were outperforming them before AI. They aren’t prompting better or doing anything magical with agent context. They are organizations with excellent paths to production.

We need to take inspiration from Dave’s story. Dave was very unhappy with his new electric car. He saved money by buying the lower-powered option, but every time he pulled away from a traffic light, he regretted that decision. Buyer’s remorse is a powerful emotional force, so Dave arranged a visit to the car dealer, who offered to upgrade him to the higher motor power option.

The upgrade was expensive, but quick. It turned out to be a feature toggle in the car’s software, so Dave had been sitting on all the technology the whole time; it had just been limited. Reluctantly, Dave handed over his hard-earned cash, and the salesman instructed Sandra, the mechanic at the dealership, to plug in her rugged laptop and flip the switch.

A wave of disappointment smacked Dave in the face as he sluggishly pulled out of the parking lot. The car didn’t feel any different. He circled the block twice and then pulled back in.

“The car doesn’t feel any different,” Dave complained to the mechanic.

“I’m not surprised,” Sandra replied. “You ought to put some tyres on those wheels.”

Just as Dave assumed his car’s performance was constrained by motor power, most organizations developing software assume that implementation time is the constraining factor for a feature. For most development teams, that’s not the case. It wasn’t before agentic AI tools like Claude Code, Cursor, or Copilot, and that means it’s even less likely to be the case now.

Just like Dave, the majority of organizations are missing the tyres that would give their wheels traction and transfer power from the motor to the road, resulting in the acceleration and velocity Dave so badly desired.

Independent studies have been telling us for a while that the gains from AI are modest at the team level, and non-existent when you roll them up to product or organizational performance. A recent report from Harvard , based on data from Jellyfish, analysed 445 million work events across coding activity, work item tracking, and work calendars. You won’t be surprised to hear the results were muted.

AI assistants have no statistically significant effect on output. AI agents do better. They do boost developer output, but this is lost downstream; just as we’d expect if we don’t use the broken model of “developers are the slowest part of software delivery”.

The Harvard study is interesting because it goes beyond “coding activity” and touches on outcomes further downstream. Still, even they don’t investigate whether the changes make any difference to software users or the organization’s balance sheet - not that this matters if the effects didn’t even make it to…

items.title: Windows Loudness Equalization, reverse-engineered and ported to PipeWire
items.content:
Windows' Loudness Equalization for PipeWire, reverse engineered from WMALFXGFXDSP.dll . It evens out the volume of each application, so quiet and loud parts play at a similar level.

modules/loudness/ : the PipeWire module and the DSP plugin. It processes every app's playback stream.

modules/limiter/ : the output limiter of Windows' audio engine ( AudioEng.dll ), on every playback device. It keeps the boost from clipping.

app/ : an optional window (GTK3) to turn it on or off, globally or per app, and set the release time.

Requires PipeWire ≥ 1.4, and GTK 3 for the window.

# Arch: sudo pacman -S pipewire gtk3 pkgconf make gcc

# Debian: sudo apt install libpipewire-0.3-dev libspa-0.2-dev libgtk-3-dev pkg-config make gcc

systemctl --user restart pipewire pipewire-pulse wireplumber

To install only one part, use make -C modules/loudness , make -C modules/limiter or make -C app . To uninstall, run sudo make uninstall and restart the same services.

Open Loudness Equalization from your application menu, or run pw-loudness-eq .

The settings live in a PipeWire metadata object, so they can also be scripted:

pw-metadata -n loudness-eq 0 enabled false # turn off

pw-metadata -n loudness-eq 0 release 6 # release time, 2 (fast) to 7 (slow)

pw-metadata -n loudness-eq 0 disabled-apps ' ["Discord"] ' Spa:String:JSON # leave these apps alone

pw-metadata -n loudness-eq # show settings

Changes apply immediately and are kept across restarts.

Defaults are in /usr/share/pipewire/pipewire.conf.d/60-loudness-eq.conf . To override them, copy it to ~/.config/pipewire/pipewire.conf.d/ .

Windows "Release Time", 2 (fast) to 7 (slow). 4 is the Windows default

Never process some apps: [ { matches = [ { application.name = "Discord" } ] actions = { loudness-eq = false } } ]

Settings changed at runtime are saved in ~/.local/state/pw-loudness-eq/state.conf and take precedence over this file.

The loudness module sets audioconvert.filter-graph.90 on each app's playback stream, so the plugin runs inside that stream, before its volume and before mixing, like a Windows stream effect.

The limiter module does what Windows' audio engine does on every playback device: after the mix and the software volume, it runs the output through a look-ahead limiter. It's always on, independent of Loudness Equalization, as on Windows.

Not processed: JACK clients, streams with more than 8 channels, and Flatpak apps that use PipeWire directly (those going through PulseAudio are processed).

A broadband automatic gain control. Despite the name, it doesn't equalize the spectrum.

Frame size N = 2^⌈log2(fs/100)⌉ (512 at 44.1/48 kHz), with 50% overlap.

Each channel is windowed with w[n] = 16384·(1 − cos(2π(n+½)/N)) / (N/2) and run through a real FFT to get the power spectrum.

Power is summed into 25 bands with edges at 100, 200, 300, 400, 510, 630, 770, 920, 1080, 1270, 1480, 1720, 2000, 2320, 2700, 3150, 3700, 4400, 5300, 6400, 7700, 9500, 12000, 15500 and 24000 Hz. Channels are summed together.

Loudness L = 1.72 · Σ max(E_b − T_b, 1e-32)^0.25 , with T = 1000, 100, 31.6, 10, 3.16, 2, 1, 1, .316, .316, 1×11, 4, 10, 100, 1000 .

Target gain = min((1300/L)^1.6, 10) , so at most +20 dB.

When the target is lower than the current gain, the gain jumps to it instantly. Otherwise it moves toward it by w = (N/128)·(44100/fs)·0.1^min(r,3)·0.316^(min(r,7)−min(r,3)) per block. At r = 4 that's a time constant of about 4.6 s.

The gain is crossfaded linearly across each half-frame. Latency is N samples.

The boost can push pure tones such as a whistle well above full scale; the limiter catches that.

Ported from CAudioLimiter in AudioEng.dll . audiodg.exe puts it on every render device, after its effects, before the device.

The output is delayed by L frames (64 at 44.1/48 kHz; 16, 32 or 128 at other rates) to look ahead. That's the device's added latency.

items.title: Taking over US Treasury subdomains for $3 each
items.content:
Elastic IP addresses (EIPs) in AWS are internet routable addresses available for use on cloud systems, by anyone. A common DNS mistake can leave them open for attackers to grab, which can lead to credential theft and worse. We demonstrated the attack is still possible in 2026, including finding real takeovers on US treasury domains, which were reported and fixed via a bug bounty program.

The cost to us for doing this was just $3 per valid takeover - what a bargain! We only covered less than 1% of the total IP space, so there are many more out there for attackers to grab. So, now is the time to review your DNS records and get those dangling records squashed ASAP.

As of the time of writing, the attack still works in practice, and though there are some controls to ban attackers abusing the system, there are sufficient gaps to make the attack practical, and at a reasonable cost.

To test how exploitable it is to claim the AWS host that a dangling DNS record points to, we needed to find a way to cycle through available EIPs with automation. The full EIP space is a maximum of ~80 million IP addresses (in practice, probably half that), and these are allocated at random, so you can’t simply claim the IP address that you want.

To do this, we’d need to repeatedly allocate and release Elastic IPs from AWS’s EC2 pool, and check each address against the DNS records in our scope.

We wanted to report any dangling records we found, so we built our target list from public bug bounty scopes.

Using the bbscope API, we pulled wildcard scope entries and passed them into subfinder to enumerate subdomains. We resolved the A records for each host and stored anything not in private or reserved ranges in a DynamoDB table for use later in our pipeline.

By default, a new AWS account can hold five Elastic IPs per region. The loop works with five, but a higher quota means more addresses per cycle. Since Service Quotas automatically approves an increase to 25 Elastic IPs per region without a support case, we requested the increase in every region.

With the quota increased, we ran a Python script to claim addresses with each cycle following this flow:

In a single region, releasing and immediately allocating a new IP often returned the same address, suggesting AWS recycles recently released addresses first. Rotating through regions gave each pool time to move on, so by the time the tool returned to the original region, it would be allocated a fresh set of IPs.

In just 48 hours, we cycled through 450,000 unique IP addresses before AWS banned the account. This was enough to find 28 live EIP takeovers in the bug bounty scope. We had covered less than 1% of the total EIP space, and already had 28 high impact findings. A determined attacker using a wider scope than bug bounty and running the campaign for an extended period of time would likely find hundreds or even thousands of DNS records that could be hijacked.

After 48 hours, our account received an abuse warning from Amazon with the action “ Blocked the ability to allocate and associate Elastic IP in all regions” . This not only stopped us from allocating new IP addresses but also from using our existing matched ones. We wanted to report our findings to customers and bug bounty programs, so we needed to be able to host PoCs on these addresses as evidence the takeover was a success.

Fortunately (or unfortunately depending on how you look at it) AWS allows you to transfer Elastic IPs between accounts, so we created a new account in our testing organization and moved the matching IPs across. It worked without any issues, despite sitting in the same organization as the banned account. New accounts under an organization can be created without going through the verification process again, so an attacker who gets an account restricted could simply spin up another account and carry on. What was the point of the ban again?

items.title: CIA hit by data breach
Schrodinger's pull requests: the 1,553 Next.js PRs with no review
items.content:
In March 2025, 255,000 people made their first open source contribution. GitHub's Octoverse report called it the largest month of first-timers in its history, and open source has only got busier since: this year's report counts 2.5 billion public contributions, more than double the year before. For anyone who wants to join in, plenty of guides say where to start. One written for beginners is also honest about why you would:

If you list open source contributions on your resume, it shows hiring managers that you have practical, real-world experience.

Arslan Ahmad, DesignGurus, 10 Must-Know Open Source Projects to Level Up Your Coding Skills as a Beginner One of its ten picks is Next.js. Yet on the 19th of November 2026, Next.js had 1,553 open pull requests that were more than a month old and had never been reviewed. A beginner's pull request joins the back of that queue.

React is on the same list, with the note that "the maintainers welcome community involvement". Still, it had 400 pull requests in the same state on that day.

I think of pull requests in that state as Schrödinger's pull requests. Schrödinger imagined a cat in a sealed box that counts as both alive and dead until someone looks. A pull request that nobody reviews is the same: neither merged nor rejected, until a maintainer opens the box.

For a newcomer, a box that stays shut costs more than time. The pull request inside can't be merged, and it gets no feedback either. So you learn nothing from it, and you have nothing to show a hiring manager. And if you were in it for the love of the project, hoping to see a few lines of your own in something millions of developers use, that doesn't happen either.

Fortunately, there are better places to start. This article lists six of them: projects that set work aside for newcomers, where a maintainer reads your pull request within days, tells you what to change and merges it when it's ready.

First, the usual advice deserves a closer look. I took a handful of the big projects that guides for beginners recommend, in lists such as DesignGurus' , Index.dev's and the awesome-for-beginners list, which has more than 91,000 stars on GitHub, and counted what happened to the pull requests that were opened by outside contributors (people who aren't public members of the project's organisation, with bots left out). The window is two months, the 21st of August to the 20th of October 2026, read on the 19th of November, so each pull request had at least 30 days to get an answer.

Project Still open a month later Never reviewed

"Still open a month later" is the share of those pull requests that has been neither merged nor closed. "Never reviewed" counts all of a project's open pull requests, drafts excluded, that are older than 30 days and have no GitHub review. Kubernetes reviewers can approve by typing /lgtm in a plain comment instead, so the last column may be less accurate for that project. If you want to know where these numbers come from, I explain it at the end of the article , with the queries and scripts I used in case you'd like to check them.

The table counts only pull requests that are still open, because a closed one at least got an answer, even if the answer was no. That covers getting a review. Finding something to work on is the other half, and the usual way in for a newcomer, a starter issue, is hard to come by too. Deno, for one, has no starter label at all. The other five have a good first issue label, yet in the last 90 days React, Next.js and scikit-learn closed no issue with that exact label, and Kubernetes closed one. PyTorch did best with 14, in a project that received more than 5,800 pull requests in two months.

Then there is the code itself. These codebases are large and complex, and the projects say so themselves. scikit-learn's contributing guide is the most direct:

Contributing to the project code generally requires advanced skills, and it may not be the best place to begin if you are new to open source…

items.title: Smart people who give a shit use tools
items.content:
Anyone who has worked on payment rails or old distributed systems knows the exact feeling Justin Michael describes in his post this week . You peel back the curtain on some piece of infrastructure the economy quietly runs on, expecting Swiss watchmaking, and find duct tape, twenty-year-old batch files, and three people in the whole company who know why you never reboot box four on a Tuesday. He calls them “smart people who give a shit,” and he’s dead right that they are the main reason the lights stay on.

Halfway down the page, though, the essay takes a turn I’ve been seeing a lot lately, and it bugs me. Michael points to the recent run of big outages (Microsoft 365, United, major banks, Apple) and blames leadership for trying to swap those people out for generative AI. Fair enough; there’s probably plenty of truth in that. But he doesn’t stop at bad management. By the end, the tools themselves have become the acid dissolving whoever picks them up. “Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out,” he writes. Every generated line robs engineers of the struggle that makes them smart and the ownership that makes them care.

The implication is pretty hard to miss: if you’re using AI, you’re giving up on giving a shit.

I use these tools every day on systems where bugs cost significant sums of money or wedge production queues, and my experience has been almost the exact opposite. More than anything else, LLMs amplify who you already are. Deeply curious, caring people can dramatically amplify what they produce and how thoroughly they understand it. Lazy bums can, for now, coast as meat proxies for a chat window, ferrying tickets into a prompt box and clicking merge on whatever falls out.

Think about what “giving a shit” actually meant on a normal engineering team before 2024. Mostly, it meant fighting a losing war against the clock. You’d spot a nasty race condition in a state machine and know you should model it in TLA+, or write a property test that hammers every interleaving, or go read the forty-thousand-line service downstream to be certain your assumption held. Half the time you didn’t, because doing it properly took two days you didn’t have and three other fires were waiting. So you eyeballed the diff, wrote a unit test for the happy path, left a slightly nervous comment, and hoped nobody touched that file for a while. Caring was rarely limited by how much people wanted to do the right thing. It was rationed by how fast one human could read and type.

When you hand a capable model to that engineer, they don’t suddenly shrug and rubber-stamp the first draft. They finally write the TLA+ spec. They pull on the threads they were always curious about, digging into why a gnarly legacy subsystem behaves the way it does instead of treating it as a black box. They build a real simulator for the flaky third-party API nobody ever had time to mock properly. They have the model trace every caller of a legacy function across a sprawling monorepo before changing its contract, instead of grepping for five minutes and praying. They write the exhaustive edge-case tests and run mutation testing against the parts that keep them awake at night.

The kind of rigor that used to be reserved for people writing avionics software or working at Bell Labs is suddenly cheap enough to pull off on an ordinary Thursday. Calling that “caring less” has the whole thing backwards.

Then there is the other side of the amplifier. Anyone who has reviewed a 1,500-line pull request written by a meat proxy who clearly hit “accept all,” got a green linter, and blanked out when asked to explain line 400 knows exactly what Michael is furious about. (I’m certainly guilty of opening massive AI-assisted PRs myself, though in the service of giving a shit, so the line count by itself isn’t the crime.) Prompt, paste, and pray is very real, and it produces miserable software. I’ve written before about the specific sinking…

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: Signal now blocks screenshots by default to keep Al agents from reading your chats
items.content:
Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years.

TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust .

In a nutshell: Signal has begun blocking screenshots by default in its messaging app. The change is aimed at AI agents that can read a phone's screen and capture sensitive information in the process. Signal argues that agents built into the operating system can bypass the end-to-end encryption that is the app's main selling point.

The company's concern is where these agents operate. Signal says Google, Apple, and Microsoft are integrating autonomous agents "deep" into their device operating systems. An agent with that level of access does not need to break an app's encryption because it can see messages, pictures, and emails after the app decrypts them for display. Any safeguards built into an individual app can therefore be bypassed.

Udbhav Tiwari, Signal's head of strategy and global affairs, put the stakes in strong terms. "The ability for billions of devices to permanently spy on their users makes the Edward Snowden revelations look like a joke," he told Politico, referring to the 2013 disclosures about mass US government surveillance.

He also raised a potential legal avenue for surveillance. Governments seeking access to private information could ask technology companies for data collected by their agents. That would eliminate the need to break encryption or install malware on a target's phone.

Apple, Google, and Microsoft declined to comment on Signal's claims. Signal wants operating system makers to give apps a way to opt out of AI data access and processing. Blocking screenshots is a temporary measure until such tools become available.

Privacy groups share the unease. Gus Hosein, executive director of Privacy International, pointed to what a phone holds. "Probably the most sensitive device in your entire life is your phone. If it gets nicked, the person stealing your phone is not going to have access to your whole life. We're undoing all those safeguards by inviting AI agents onto these devices," he said.

Telegram now lets developers turn chats into interactive mini apps

Researchers found a way to eavesdrop on headphones from 30 meters away, and encryption can't stop it

Itxaso Domínguez de Olazábal, a policy adviser at the European digital rights group EDRi, called for "serious limits" on what agents can access. She described a future in which "the companies controlling our operating systems can effectively decide how much privacy we are allowed to have, even when we deliberately choose services designed to protect it."

Operating-system-level agents have already launched in many countries. Their rollout has been slower in the European Union, where Apple has cited the bloc's digital competition rules as a key obstacle to introducing its newest AI assistant features. Meta is also advancing its own agent, Muse, which has launched in the United Kingdom.

The UK's Information Commissioner's Office warned last month that AI agent products "may amplify and accelerate risks" to consumers. It said this week that Meta committed to a "voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme" so regulators can keep watching the product. The office is also preparing new guidance on how privacy law applies to AI agents. Meta says Muse is "private, safe and secure by design" and that it has "engaged constructively" with regulators.

Beyond the most serious privacy risks, there are also concerns about what happens to data once an agent gains access to it. Critics worry that the information could be repurposed for AI training or targeted advertising.

Regulators are focusing on one particularly difficult aspect of this problem: data belonging to people who have never interacted with the agent. Third-party data includes messages and holiday pictures sent to a friend who has quietly allowed an AI agent to access their conversations. The sender may have no idea their information is being collected.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.
